full_query:
A 26-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a 6-month history of increasing lower back pain. He first felt the pain while lifting boxes at work but thought that he had just strained a muscle. The pain appears to be worse in the mornings and after rest. Exercise and physical activity appear to temporarily make the pain better. He has taken acetaminophen and ibuprofen for the pain. He has no significant medical history and takes no medications. His temperature is 98.6°F (37.0°C), blood pressure is 115/70 mmHg, pulse is 70/min, and respirations are 12/min. On physical exam, he is found to have limited flexion and extension of his spine as well as tenderness to palpation over the insertion of his patellar tendons bilaterally. Results from laboratory tests are shown below:

Serum:
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 61 mm/hr
C-reactive protein (CRP): 36 mg/L (normal <10 mg/L)

Which of the following is the most accurate test for this patient's condition? (A) Bone scan (B) Computed tomography (C) Magnetic resonance imaging (D) Radiograph (E) Ultrasound

shared_context.exam: limited flexion and extension of spine, tenderness to palpation over patellar tendon insertion bilaterally

sentences: To determine the most accurate test for this patient's condition, we need to analyze the clinical presentation, physical examination findings, and laboratory results step-by-step
A 26-year-old man with a 6-month history of increasing lower back pain
Pain worsens in the mornings and after rest
Pain is temporarily relieved with exercise and physical activity
No significant medical history and no ongoing medications
Morning stiffness and improvement with activity are characteristic symptoms of inflammatory back pain
Limited flexion and extension of the spine
Tenderness over the insertion of the patellar tendons bilaterally
Limited spinal mobility and tenderness at tendon insertion sites are suggestive of enthesitis, commonly seen in spondyloarthropathies
Elevated ESR (61 mm/hr) and elevated CRP (36 mg/L)
Elevated ESR and CRP are indicative of an inflammatory process
The combination of chronic lower back pain, morning stiffness, improvement with activity, enthesitis, and elevated inflammatory markers is highly suggestive of Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS)
Ankylosing Spondylitis typically presents with chronic back pain that improves with exercise and is associated with enthesitis and elevated inflammatory markers
To confirm the diagnosis of Ankylosing Spondylitis, imaging studies are crucial
Radiographs (X-rays) are typically the initial imaging modality to look for changes in the sacroiliac joints
However, plain radiographs may not detect early changes
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is more sensitive and can detect early inflammatory changes such as bone marrow edema, which are not visible on X-rays
MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality for detecting early sacroiliitis and other inflammatory changes in Ankylosing Spondylitis
Based on this analysis, the most accurate test for diagnosing this patient's condition is
Option C: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
(C) Magnetic resonance imaging
